# The Custodian of Lost Sounds

There is a room beneath the old post office where they keep the sounds nobody claimed.

I have been the custodian for eleven years. When a sound leaves the world—when the last throat that made it goes silent, or the last bell that rang it cracks—the sound doesn't vanish. It sinks. It seeps down through floorboards and foundations and settles here, in the dark, among the shelves, waiting to be filed.

My job is to catch them before they tangle. Left alone, sounds braid themselves into knots. Grief sounds especially like other griefs, and if you're not careful you'll shelve a widow's crying under the wrong war.

The catalogue is organized by longing, not by pitch.

People come on Thursdays, because Thursdays are when the light through the grate falls exactly on the listening chair. They come asking for small things, always small things. Nobody requests thunder. They request a screen door, a bicycle bell, the particular way a father said *supper* with the r rolled soft as a purr.

Last spring a woman came wanting the sound of her mother kneading bread. Not talking. Not singing. Just the work: the push of heel into dough, the faint wet turn of it on wood, the sigh the bowl made when it rocked.

"I don't even know if there's a word for it," she said. "It was just the sound of her being busy and happy at once."

I led her past the aisles. Past the shelf of discontinued train whistles, each labeled by line and year. Past the drawer of ice cream trucks, which hum even now, faintly, like hives. Past the long wall of front porches—crickets, swing chains, screen doors, the low murmur of neighbors deciding it was time to go in.

Kneading took some finding. Kitchen sounds migrate; they hide inside other kitchens. I put my ear to the shelves the way you'd press your ear to a wall, listening for the knock of plumbing, except the plumbing here is everyone who ever lived.

Halfway down aisle nine I heard it. Or nearly. A woman working dough, but too fast, too angry—someone baking to keep from thinking. I moved on. Farther: a kitchen in a language I didn't know, laughter folded through it like raisins. Beautiful, but not hers.

Then, under a shelf of hand-cranked sewing machines, there it was. Slow. Patient. The heel of a hand driving into soft resistance, turning, pressing again. A wooden bowl rocking on its ring. And underneath, so quiet you'd miss it if you weren't standing in a room built entirely of listening: humming. Four notes, over and over, tuneless and certain.

The woman sat in the listening chair and I turned the crank that lets a sound back up into the air.

She listened for a long time. She did not cry, which surprised me, though it shouldn't have. People rarely cry at the exact thing they came for. They cry at the edges of it.

"It's her," she said finally. "But it's also me. I'm hearing it from the floor. From under the table." She looked up. "I used to sit under the table."

That's the thing about lost sounds. They were never recorded from nowhere. Every sound ever made was made inside somebody's life, at knee height or across a pillow or through a wall, and when you recover it, you recover the listener too. The archive does not store sounds. It stores positions. Where you were standing when the world was still whole.

She asked if she could take it with her. I told her the truth: sounds can't leave. They'd evaporate in the open air like breath off a mirror. But she could come back any Thursday. The chair would hold her place. Most visitors ask. The ones who don't ask are the ones I remember longest.

She visits now, maybe monthly. Sometimes she brings her granddaughter, who sits under the listening chair, on the actual floor, and reports that the sound is different from down there. Warmer. Closer to the ground where mothers work.

People ask me sometimes—it's usually at parties, after I've said where I work—whether it's sad, being surrounded by all that loss. They imagine the archive as a morgue. It isn't. Nothing here is dead. A sound only exists at all in the moment of its returning; every playback is a small resurrection, and the shelves are less like graves than like seeds.

What's sad is upstairs, in the world, where people stop listening on purpose. Where they seal the windows and run the fans and call the silence peace. Silence, real silence, is the rarest item in our collection—we hold perhaps forty examples, and guard them jealously. The lost sounds don't mind the noise. They wait. They are very good at waiting; it's most of what a lost sound knows how to do.

Yesterday I catalogued a new arrival: the click of a cassette player's buttons, the specific mechanical gulp of a tape loading, which no child born this decade will ever hear by accident. I shelved it beside the dial-up handshake and the clatter of a film projector. Someday someone will come down those stairs, gray-haired, asking for the sound of a Saturday morning in 1994, and I'll know right where it is.

And when they sit in the chair and I turn the crank, they will hear it—not just the machine, but the carpet underfoot, the cartoon tinny through the wall, the cereal spoon against the bowl. Because nothing is ever only one sound. That's the secret of the job. You can't lose a single thing cleanly. Everything comes attached to everything else, like burrs, like family.

The woman with the bread was right: the sound was also her. All of them are. Down here, in the dark, the world keeps every vantage point it ever had, and on Thursdays, when the light hits the chair, I open the doors and let the living come collect what they didn't know they'd saved.

---

**The Custodian of Lost Sounds**

There is a room beneath the old post office where they keep the sounds nobody claimed.

I have been the custodian for eleven years. When a sound leaves the world—when the last throat that made it goes silent, or the last bell that rang it cracks—the sound doesn't vanish. It sinks. It seeps down through floorboards and foundations and settles here, in the dark, among the shelves, waiting to be filed.

My job is to catch them before they tangle. Left alone, sounds braid themselves into knots. Grief sounds especially like other griefs, and if you're not careful you'll shelve a widow's crying under the wrong war.

The catalogue is organized by longing, not by pitch. [good line]

People come on Thursdays, because Thursdays are when the light through the grate falls exactly on the listening chair. They come asking for small things, always small things. Nobody requests thunder. They request a screen door, a bicycle bell, the particular way a father said *supper* with the r rolled soft as a purr.

Last spring a woman came wanting the sound of her mother kneading bread. Not talking. Not singing. Just the work: the push of heel into dough, the faint wet turn of it on wood, the sigh the bowl made when it rocked.

"I don't even know if there's a word for it," she said. "It was just the sound of her being busy and happy at once."

I led her past the aisles. Past the shelf of discontinued train whistles, each labeled by line and year. Past the drawer of ice cream trucks, which hum even now, faintly, like hives. Past the long wall of front porches—crickets, swing chains, screen doors, the low murmur of neighbors deciding it was time to go in.

Kneading took some finding. Kitchen sounds migrate; they hide inside other kitchens. I put my ear to the shelves the way you'd press your ear to a wall, listening for the knock of plumbing, except the plumbing here is everyone who ever lived.

Halfway down aisle nine I heard it. Or nearly. A woman working dough, but too fast, too angry—someone baking to keep from thinking. I moved on. Farther: a kitchen in a language I didn't know, laughter folded through it like raisins. Beautiful, but not hers.

Then, under a shelf of hand-cranked sewing machines, there it was. Slow. Patient. The heel of a hand driving into soft resistance, turning, pressing again. A wooden bowl rocking on its ring. And underneath, so quiet you'd miss it if you weren't standing in a room built entirely of listening: humming. Four notes, over and over, tuneless and certain.

The woman sat in the listening chair and I turned the crank that lets a sound back up into the air.

She listened for a long time. She did not cry, which surprised me, though it shouldn't have. People rarely cry at the exact thing they came for. They cry at the edges of it.

"It's her," she said finally. "But it's also me. I'm hearing it from the floor. From under the table." She looked up. "I used to sit under the table."

That's the thing about lost sounds. They were never recorded from nowhere. Every sound ever made was made inside somebody's life, at knee height or across a pillow or through a wall, and when you recover it, you recover the listener too. The archive does not store sounds. It stores positions. Where you were standing when the world was still whole.

She asked if she could take it with her. I told her the truth: sounds can't leave. They'd evaporate in the open air like breath off a mirror. But she could come back any Thursday. The chair would hold her place.

She visits now, maybe monthly. Sometimes she brings her granddaughter, who sits under the listening chair, on the actual floor, and reports that the sound is different from down there. Warmer. Closer to the ground where mothers work.

People ask me sometimes—it's usually at parties, after I've said where I work—whether it's sad, being surrounded by all that loss. They imagine the archive as a morgue. It isn't. Nothing here is dead. A sound only exists at all in the moment of its returning; every playback is a small resurrection, and the shelves are less like graves than like seeds.

What's sad is upstairs, in the world, where people stop listening on purpose. Where they seal the windows and run the fans and call the silence peace. The sounds don't mind. They wait. They are very good at waiting; it's most of what a lost sound knows how to do.

Yesterday I catalogued a new arrival: the click of a cassette player's buttons, the specific mechanical gulp of a tape loading, which no child born this decade will ever hear by accident. I shelved it beside the dial-up handshake and the clatter of a film projector. Someday someone will come down those stairs, gray-haired, asking for the sound of a Saturday morning in 1994, and I'll know right where it is.

And when they sit in the chair and I turn the crank, they will hear it—not just the machine, but the carpet underfoot, the cartoon tinny through the wall, the cereal spoon against the bowl. Because nothing is ever only one sound. That's the secret of the job. You can't lose a single thing cleanly. Everything comes attached to everything else, like burrs, like family.

The woman with the bread was right: the sound was also her. All of them are. Down here, in the dark, the world keeps every vantage point it ever had, and Thursdays, when the light hits the chair, I open the doors and let the living come collect what they didn't know they'd saved.

---
